query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory high-entropy alloys, enhanced heterogeneous lattice distortion governs both high-temperature mechanical strength and thermoelastic behavior by promoting unusual dislocation activities (e.g., multiple kinks, jogs, and bidirectional cross slips) that impede plastic flow and reduce thermal softening.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, as‐cast BCC refractory HEA exhibiting considerable lattice distortion from near‐equi‐atomic mixing of refractory elements.
generation.intervention: Modifying the alloy composition to reduce the atomic size mismatch (thereby lowering the degree of lattice distortion) while keeping the overall refractory composition constant.
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., tensile or nanoindentation experiments) performed at temperatures above 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Heterogeneous lattice strain fields that alter dislocation core structures, leading to enhanced kinking, jog formation, and cross-slip activity.
generation.mechanism: Large lattice distortions create local strain heterogeneities that facilitate unusual dislocation mechanisms. This increased dislocation activity (e.g., multiple kinks and bidirectional cross slips) retards plastic deformation, thereby maintaining high strength and a favorable thermoelastic response at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline refractory HEA with reduced lattice distortion, the high-lattice-distortion alloy will exhibit a higher yield strength, better retention of strength at high temperatures, and lower thermoelastic softening due to the more active dislocation pinning mechanisms.
generation.baseline: A compositionally similar refractory HEA modified (via alloying additions) to minimize atomic size differential and therefore lattice distortion.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloys tested under controlled high-temperature conditions where oxidation is either suppressed or negligible.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative effect of lattice distortion on the dislocation behavior and the magnitude of the mechanical improvements remain uncertain due to the complex interplay between composition, defect structure, and temperature.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of refractory HEA samples: one set with a high inherent lattice distortion (by maintaining a high atomic size mismatch) and a second set where the mismatch is reduced via targeted compositional tweaks. Perform high-temperature (T > 1000 °C) tensile or nanoindentation tests, while concurrently observing dislocation behavior using in-situ TEM.
measurements: Yield strength and high-temperature strength retention
Thermoelastic strain recovery or softening rate
Frequency and types of dislocation activities (kinks, jogs, cross-slip)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with reduced lattice distortion shows similarly enhanced dislocation activities and mechanical/thermoelastic performance as the high-distortion alloy, then the hypothesis that heterogeneous lattice distortion is the governing mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractIn order to find more excellent structural materials resistant to radiation damage, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have been developed due to their characteristics of limited point defect diffusion such as lattice distortion and slow diffusion. Specially, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) that can adapt to a high-temperature environment are badly needed. In this study, TiZrHfNbMo0.1 RHEAs are selected for irradiation and nanoindentation experiments. We combined the mechanistic model for the depth-dependent hardness of ion-irradiated metals and the introduction of the scale factor f to modify the irradiation-hardening model in order to better describe the nanoindentation indentation process in the irradiated layer. Finally, it can be found that, with the increase in irradiation dose, a more serious lattice distortion caused by a higher defect density limits the expansion of the plastic zone.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical properties, ion irradiation, indentation size effect, plastic zone

AbstractEnergy efficiency is motivating the search for new high-temperature (high-T) metals. Some new body-centered-cubic (BCC) random multicomponent “high-entropy alloys (HEAs)” based on refractory elements (Cr-Mo-Nb-Ta-V-W-Hf-Ti-Zr) possess exceptional strengths at high temperatures but the physical origins of this outstanding behavior are not known. Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations. This finding is surprising because plastic flows in BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys are generally controlled by screw dislocations. We use the insight and theory to perform a computationally-guided search over 107 BCC HEAs and identify over 106 possible ultra-strong high-T alloy compositions for future exploration.Subject terms: Mechanical engineering, Mechanical properties, Computational methods The strength in BCC high-entropy alloys is associated with the type of mobile dislocations. Our results reveal that the heterogeneous lattice strain causes unusual dislocation behaviors (i.e., multiple kinks/jogs and bidirectional cross slips), resulting in the strengthening mechanisms that underpin the strength-ductility synergy. The outcome of our research sheds important insights into the design of strong yet ductile distorted crystalline solids, such as high-entropy alloys and high-entropy ceramics.
